Project

Glossary

This page defines the terms that the other pages of the plugin manual use. Each entry gives the meaning in the contract ilium:plugin@0.1.0. Where a term has a page of its own, the entry links to it. Read this page first when a term is unfamiliar.

A plugin is a WebAssembly component that the host loads, checks and runs. It reacts to events, sends intents that change Ilium, and uses only the rights that the user has granted. Most terms below describe one of four things: the package that carries the plugin, the rights it holds, the calls it makes, and the lifecycle that runs it.

You will need

  • Nothing installed, to read this page.
  • To write a plugin, the toolchain from Getting started: toolchain. The ilium plugin commands are part of the ilium binary, so installing Ilium installs them.
  • A Rust or TypeScript project. The examples below use the SDK import paths from the API pages.
  • Basic familiarity with JSON, because the manifest is a JSON file.

Terms

Action. A user interaction with a widget, delivered to the client side as a ui-action event with a kind, such as activated or changed, and a value. See Events and intents.

Activation. The moment the host instantiates a plugin and calls lifecycle.activate. A plugin is activated at startup, on the first use of one of its contributions, or on one of the triggers in its manifest activation list. See Lifecycle.

Authorization epoch. A counter that the host increases each time a grant is revoked or added. A host call compares the epoch it started with against the current one. A call that is still in flight when the epoch changes returns revoked.

Bundle. A folder that holds signed registry metadata and the packages of chosen plugins, copied to a machine with no network. ilium plugin export-bundle writes it and install --from-bundle reads it. See Registry reference.

Capability. A named right that a plugin requests in its manifest and the user grants. Each host import and each event is behind one. See Capability table.

Channel. A release track of a plugin, stable or beta. A plugin follows one channel for updates. See Versions and dependencies.

Component. A WebAssembly component: the compiled form of one side of a plugin, named server.wasm, client.wasm or scene.wasm. A package holds one component per side that the plugin uses. See Rust SDK and TypeScript SDK.

Contribution. Something a plugin adds to Ilium: a command, a keybinding, a settings page, a panel, a pane kind, a decoration slot, a scene or a help topic. A static contribution is declared in the manifest. A dynamic one is pushed at runtime. See Manifest reference.

.cwasm. A WebAssembly component that has already been compiled for the host. The release embeds the bundled first-party plugins in this form, so they start without a compile step. See Design decisions.

Decoration. A short styled text or a Tabler icon that a plugin sets on a tree row, in a slot that the manifest declares, such as a badge or a footer. A decoration with persist: true survives a server restart, marked as stale. See Manifest reference.

De-duplication key. The optional dedup-key field of a submission: 1 to 128 characters from [A-Za-z0-9._:/-]. A submission whose key the same plugin reserved within the last 10 minutes completes as duplicate(original) and has no effect. A refused submission does not reserve its key. The Rust helper dedup::key_for joins its parts with :. A send-input or agent-action submission must carry a key. See Events and intents.

Deprecate. To mark a whole plugin as no longer maintained, with an optional successor. Installs still work. See Registry reference.

Editor primitive. The host-provided pane kind for editing text. It is native. A plugin may provide an editor only after v1. See Design decisions.

Extension point. A named slot that one plugin owns and others fill. A collect point gathers data entries. A hook point runs handlers from other plugins in the owner's flow, in one of four modes: observe, transform, veto or first. Its id is <plugin-id>/<point>. See Extension points.

Grant. The user's approval of one capability for one side of a plugin. A grant string is a name, or a name with an argument, such as fs.read:project. See Capability table.

Hook. A handler that a plugin contributes to a hook point. It answers pass, replace, refuse or answer, within a short deadline. A hook that is late or fails counts as pass. See Extension points.

Host. The Ilium code that loads plugins, checks their calls and runs them. The host is the kernel together with the plugin host.

.iliumpkg. The one package format for plugins. It is a deterministic ZIP archive that holds a manifest, one or more components, assets, help topics and a file inventory. It replaces the old .iliumanim format. See Packages and Porting from .iliumanim.

Intent. A request that a plugin sends to change Ilium, such as rename-node or send-input. An intent travels inside a submission. Each submission completes with exactly one outcome. See Events and intents.

Job. A unit of background work that a plugin starts with jobs.start. A job runs the job-runner.run export in a second instance of the same component, with its own deadline and memory limit. The plugin reads the result with take-output. See Background jobs.

Kernel. The part of Ilium that is native code and not a plugin (tier T0). It owns the tree, the panes, the settings store, the snapshot and the recovery page.

Key id. The fingerprint of a publisher public key: the SHA-256 of the key bytes, written as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters in 16 groups of 4. See Signing and trust.

Lock file. The file ilium-plugins.lock in a project. It records the exact version and package hash of each plugin, so install --locked gives the same set everywhere. See Versions and dependencies.

Mirror. A copy of a registry on another host or share. Clients check the signatures of the original registry, never the mirror operator. See Registry reference.

Namespace. The first part of a plugin id, such as com.example, that one publisher owns in a registry. See Registry reference.

Outcome. The result of a submission: ok, ok-node, ok-epoch, duplicate, refused, failed or cancelled. See the table in Reference values.

Pane. A node of the tree that shows a running process, an agent, an editor or a plugin's own view.

Pin. To hold a plugin at one version so that updates skip it. See Distribution commands.

Preopen. A directory that the host opens for a granted file scope and passes to the component through WASI. A plugin sees only the preopens of the scopes it was granted, such as /project or /data.

Primitive. A host-provided pane kind that a plugin can build on or extend. The four primitives are terminal, agent, editor and basic, imported from ilium_plugin_sdk::primitives in Rust. See Primitives.

Provider. A plugin that supplies a service to others: a service provider for a named interface, or an inference provider for model calls. The host routes calls to the provider. See Services.

Publisher id. The identifier of a publisher, stored with the signing key and equal to the start of every plugin id that the key signs. It is different from the display name in publisher. See Signing and trust.

Registry. An optional source of plugins: signed JSON files and package blobs on an HTTPS host or file share. Ilium ships with none configured (decision D27). See Registry reference.

Replacement. A plugin that lists another plugin in replaces and provides its whole surface. The replaced core plugin is turned off while the replacement is on. See Extending core plugins.

Reproducible build. A build in which two machines make the same package bytes from the same source. See Publishing guide.

Restored state. The bytes that a plugin returns from deactivate. The host stores them and passes them back as restored on the next activation. The limit is 1 MiB. Larger bytes are dropped, and the next activation receives no value.

Retained mode. The rule that plugins run when an event arrives or a timer fires, and push their state to the host. The host keeps that state and draws it. A plugin's views.render is not called on every frame. See Retained mode.

SBOM. Software bill of materials: a list of the libraries inside a component, kept in sbom.json. See Publishing guide.

Scene. An animated background, written as a scene component that implements the renderer export. A scene draws into a surface, and the host applies the shared look to the result. See Scenes.

Scope. A named area of the file system that an fs.* grant refers to, such as project, data or cache. See File access.

Shared look. The colour, style and dithering settings that the user sets once and the host applies to every scene and surface. A plugin does not add its own brightness or palette controls. See Accessibility and theming.

Side. One of the three places a plugin runs: server (S), client (C) or scene (A, animation). Each side has its own component, grant list, instance, state and failure count. See Worlds and sides.

Surface. A pixel buffer that a plugin writes into. It is shown either by a surface widget or as the frame of a scene. The formats are listed in Reference values.

Tier. The trust level of a plugin: T0 for the kernel, T1 for bundled first-party code, T2 for signed third-party code and T3 for unsigned local code. See Security model.

Tree. The hierarchy of nodes that Ilium shows in the sidebar, made of groups and panes.

Trust store. The file in which the host keeps the publisher keys that the user or administrator trusts, each with a tier. See Signing and trust.

Widget. One visual element of a plugin's view, such as a block, a paragraph, a table or a tabs widget. See the widget pages, starting with Widgets index.

WIT. The WebAssembly Interface Types language. The plugin contract is written in WIT, and the Rust and TypeScript bindings are generated from it. Names stay kebab-case in WIT. The SDKs convert them, as shown in the naming rule below.

World. The WIT name for the set of imports and exports that one component may use, such as ilium:server/base@0.1.0. A manifest names the world of each component.

Yank. To withdraw one version from new installs and updates while installed copies keep working. See Registry reference.

Further terms

Cookbook. The set of tested recipes in Patterns cookbook: debounce, throttle, cache, retry and others.

Data version. The integer data_version in the manifest. A change makes the host run migrator before activate. See Data migration.

Display width. The number of terminal cells a text takes. Wide characters take two. Measured with display-width. See Internationalisation.

Fingerprint. The SHA-256 of a raw publisher public key, shown in the trust dialog. See Publishing and support.

Anchor. A named place in a built-in Settings tab where a plugin section can attach. Anchors are only ever added. See Plugin settings extension.

Attention mark. A flag on a node set with mark-attention and cleared with ack-attention, behind the grant tree.attention. It drives the Attention display mode.

Catalogue. A named, typed list of options that a choice row or a widget uses as its source. A plugin declares its own in catalogs. The host serves read-only ones named ilium.*, such as ilium.palettes.

Chrome. The parts of the client around the content: tree toolbar, row actions, status bar segments and pane frame slots. A plugin fills them with the grant ui.chrome.

Client request. A call from one side of a plugin to its other side, declared in client_requests and sent with client.request. It is always granted and reaches only the plugin's own sides.

Consent prompt. A question the host asks the user at the first use of something that is not a grant by itself: the first geocoding lookup, the first open-external to each origin, and the first request to a host taken from a setting. See Security model.

Durable timer. A timer made with timers.at that survives a restart. It fires once, late, as durable-timer-fired.

First-party limits tier. The value "first-party" of the manifest key limits_tier. It raises the settings caps and is allowed only for bundled ilium.* plugins (error manifest.limits-tier).

Frame slot. A place in a pane frame (header icon, header text, footer row or banner) that a plugin fills with set-frame-slot.

High-risk grant (H). A grant that is off by default in every dialog and always needs an explicit user choice, even for a bundled plugin. Eleven grants are high risk in the contract; settings.read-kernel is high only for the api tab.

Host catalogue. A catalogue owned by the kernel, such as ilium.palettes, ilium.dithers, ilium.filters, ilium.style-presets or ilium.icons.

Input journal. The record of send-input submissions made with journal: true. An entry without a recorded outcome after a crash is reported once as input-uncertain and never replayed.

Intent, lifecycle. An intent that changes a pane's process: freeze-pane, unfreeze-pane, replace-pane-command, terminate-pane-process or resize-pane. It needs panes.lifecycle.

Limits tier. The class of caps that apply to a plugin: standard, or first-party for bundled plugins.

Long-lived child. A process started with process.spawn that keeps running and streams output as events. It needs process.long-lived and a matching process.run:<program> grant.

Prompt epoch. A counter of the prompts sent to an agent pane. ok-epoch returns the new value.

Restructure batch. A group of tree changes sent with the intent restructure, applied atomically and undone with revert-restructure. Undo tokens do not survive a restart.

Row state. The enabled, disabled or hidden state of a settings row, set with settings.set-row-state or computed from visible_when.

Section. A block of settings rows that a plugin adds to a tab. In a built-in tab it sits under a divider that names the plugin.

Snapshot, frozen. A copy of a terminal screen taken with terminal.freeze-snapshot so that a plugin reads one consistent state.

Token provider. An optional export that supplies syntax tokens for a language declared in languages.

Toast. A short message drawn by the client, sent with the intent toast (grant notify.toast).

Unstable feature. An item marked @unstable(feature = <name>). It is visible only to a plugin that lists the name in unstable and only in development builds for T2 and T3. gpu.kernels is one.

Plugin host. The part of Ilium that loads components, links their imports, runs their exports under deadlines and enforces their limits. It is the crate ilium-plugin-host, and one instance of it runs in each process that hosts plugins. See Host architecture.

Dispatcher. The task inside a plugin host that takes events, intents and calls from the kernel, batches them, and hands each call to the plugin executor in priority order. See Host scheduling.

Execution quota group. The token bucket ilium-execution of one plugin side: 2,000 ms of CPU time that refills at 500 ms per second. An empty bucket makes submissions return quota-exceeded. See Errors and limits.

Worker bank. The pool of threads, min(4, cores / 2) and at least one, that runs background job instances so that jobs never block the plugin executor. See Background jobs.

Store and instance. In Wasmtime, a Store holds the memory and state of one running copy of a component, called an instance. Ilium uses one Store per plugin side instance. See Host runtime.

Epoch tick. A 10 ms step of the engine clock that Wasmtime uses to interrupt running guest code. The host sets the deadline to ceil(d / 10) + 1 ticks after the call starts, so a guest that spins traps no earlier than d and no later than d + 20 ms. See Host runtime.

Sandbox helper. The separate process ilium-plugin-helper that hosts one T2 or T3 plugin side inside a Linux sandbox. See Sandbox helper protocol.

World variant. A base world (server/base, client/base, anim/base) plus the optional export fragments, such as with-hook-handler, that a plugin implements. See Worlds and sides.

Plugin envelope. The record PluginEnvelope that carries plugin traffic between a client and the server on the existing connection: submissions, outcomes, messages and control. See Plugin traffic over IPC.

Contribution delta. The record ContributionDelta that carries changes of retained contributions (decorations, status segments, virtual rows) from the server to each client, as a snapshot followed by numbered increments. See Plugin traffic over IPC.

Caller deadline. The timeout the caller sets on a request, for example the timeout_millis of an HTTP call or the client-request timeout. When it passes, the caller gets timed-out. See Reply deadlines.

Ceiling. The largest value a tier may use for a limits key. The host clamps a request above the ceiling and logs it. See Errors and limits reference.

Grace. The 100 ms after a soft deadline. A call that is still running when the grace ends traps. See Host scheduling.

Hard deadline. A deadline at which the host interrupts the call. The call traps and counts as a failure unless its call class says it does not. See Host scheduling.

host-capacity. The reason shown when the host refuses to start an instance because of session limits, such as the memory pool or the helper count. It is not a failure. See Errors and limits reference.

Near-miss. A call that ended within its deadline but used at least 80% of it. See Health and watchdog.

retry-after-ms. A field of the plugin-error record. On quota-exceeded and rate-limited it says how long to wait before the same call can succeed. See Errors and limits reference.

Soft deadline. A deadline that does not interrupt the call. The call finishes, the host discards a late result, and the breach counts toward the streak limit. See Host scheduling.

Streak limit. The number of consecutive soft-deadline breaches of one call class that trap the instance: 3, or 30 for scene frames. See Host scheduling.

Trap. The instance aborts. The host counts one failure and restarts the side after 1 s, then 5 s, and disables it at the third failure within 10 minutes. See Errors and limits reference.

ABI fault and semantic fault. An ABI fault is a breach of the binary contract, such as a bad pointer or a malformed record, and traps the instance. A semantic fault is a valid call that the host refuses, and it returns an error code to the plugin. See Errors and limits reference.

Internal decision ids

Some pages cite short ids such as L2 to L6, AX5, E9 and C78. They come from the design notes. L2 to L6 are section labels in Errors and limits reference, and AX5 is a decision in Design decisions. E9 and C78 have no page that defines them, and a reader can ignore them. The requirement ids written in square brackets with a prefix and a number are the ones that tests use.

For users

These terms appear in the Plugins tab, in dialogs and in ilium plugin list. Each entry says what the word means for a person who installs and manages plugins. The longer pages are Plugins for users, Install and manage plugins and Permissions explained.

Term What it means for you
Plugin A small program that adds a feature to Ilium. Thirty come with Ilium. Others are installed from a .iliumpkg file.
Core plugin A plugin that comes with Ilium and has an id that starts with ilium.core.. Badge T1. See Core plugins for users.
Package One .iliumpkg file. Ilium has no store. You get the file from the author.
Permission The plain-language name of a grant: one thing a plugin may do, such as read files in this project. You answer for each one when you install.
High risk A permission that can read private data or change things outside Ilium. It starts unchecked.
Signed The package carries a signature from a publisher key. Badge T2.
Unsigned, dev The package has no signature. Badge T3 and dev. Install it only if you built it or reviewed it.
Publisher key The key you trust to sign packages. You see its short fingerprint when you trust it.
On, Off, Failed The state words in the Plugins tab. They are defined in Settings, plugin rows.
Blocked by policy An administrator rule forbids the plugin. See Administration.
Safe mode A start of Ilium with third-party plugins off for that run. See Troubleshooting plugins.
Recovery page The simple plugin page that works when Settings does not.

Reference values

Tiers

Tier Who writes it How it is loaded Install rule
T0 The kernel Native code Not a plugin
T1 First-party, bundled Precompiled .cwasm Granted the manifest ceiling, except high-risk grants
T2 Third parties, signed .iliumpkg with an Ed25519 signature Review dialog, normal grants checked
T3 Local, unsigned .iliumpkg without a signature Review dialog, normal grants checked

Windows and macOS refuse T2 and T3 packages until a sandbox exists on those systems. The refusal reads: Cannot install <name> <version>. followed by Third-party plugins need the plugin sandbox, which is not available on Windows yet. and Bundled plugins keep working.

Sides and worlds

Side Component file Base world
S, server server.wasm ilium:server/base@0.1.0
C, client client.wasm ilium:client/base@0.1.0
A, animation scene.wasm ilium:anim/base@0.1.0

Outcomes

Outcome Meaning
ok The submission was applied. For a call, the typed result is ready to take.
ok-node(node-id) The submission was applied and created this node.
ok-epoch(u64) A send-input on an agent pane was applied and carries the new prompt epoch. The SDK treats it as ok where code matches only ok.
duplicate(original) The dedup key was reserved. original is the reference of the first submission.
refused(code) Not applied, for a check that ran before acceptance. The key is not reserved.
failed(code) Accepted, but the host failed to apply it, for example with io or timed-out.
cancelled Stopped by the plugin, the user, or a shutdown. (A sibling of a refused submission is refused(cancelled), not cancelled.)

Error codes

Code Meaning Retry
not-permitted No capability, the user declined it, or the path leaves its scope No
not-found The node, pane, file, command, plugin or other named thing is gone No
invalid-argument The call breaks a rule the plugin can check, such as a size cap No, fix the call
conflict The state changed, or a lock or claim is held Yes, after re-reading the state
quota-exceeded A stored or held quota is full After freeing resources
rate-limited A rate rule throttles the call Yes, after retry-after-ms
busy Transient capacity is full Yes, later
timed-out A deadline passed Yes
cancelled The request was cancelled Maybe
unsupported The host or platform cannot do it No
pane-not-ready A restored terminal pane has not started its process Yes, after the pane event
revoked The authorization epoch changed during the call No, the plugin is re-activated
io An operating system I/O error other than a missing file Maybe
network DNS, connect, TLS or transport failure Yes
internal A host bug, or a trap inside a job No

Grants

A grant string is name or name:argument. The first colon separates the name from the argument, so later colons belong to the argument.

Grant Meaning
agent.read Read agent state. No argument.
fs.read:project Read the project directory, mounted as /project.
http:api.example.com Call one exact host.
http:*.example.com Call any subdomain, at any depth. The bare domain is not included.
process.run:git Run the program git, resolved through PATH.
topics.subscribe:build/* Receive every topic under the prefix build/.

Grants are recorded per plugin, per side, and per user configuration. They are not recorded per project. A high-risk grant (H) is never checked by default in the install dialog.

File scopes and preopens

Scope Preopen Default
package /package Always, read only
data /data Always, read and write
cache /cache Always, read and write, evictable
project /project Granted
picked /picked/<n> Granted per pick
path:<template> /paths/<n> Granted, high risk for a literal absolute path

Templates can start with {home}, {config}, {data}, {cache}, {project} or {worktrees}.

Activation triggers

startup, event:<event-name>, command:<id>, view:<id>, pane-kind:<id>, scene:<id>, cli:<name>, http:<path>, service:<interface>, topic:<topic> and settings:<tab-id>. Without an activation list, a plugin is activated on the first use of any of its contributions.

Deactivation reasons

Reason When it happens
shutdown The server or client stops. The plugin has its deactivate deadline (500 ms by default).
disabled The user or plugins.set-enabled turns the plugin off.
upgrade An update or ilium plugin dev replaces the running version.
crash-restart Declared in the WIT enum but never delivered: a trap drops the instance without a call.
revoked A capability was revoked. The plugin is re-activated with fewer grants.
granted A capability was added. The plugin is re-activated with more grants.
detached Not a deactivation reason. A client that disconnects cleanly deactivates its instance with shutdown, and the instance returns restore bytes for the next attach.

Surface formats

Use Formats
A scene surface (ilium:anim/surface) gray8, rgb8, rgba8
A surface widget mask8, mono1, gray8, rgb8, rgba8

A scene row is width bytes for gray8, 3 x width for rgb8 and 4 x width for rgba8.

Worked examples

Rust: a keyed submission

This server-side function builds a submission that sets a badge on one node. The key names the node and the change. The same change sent again within 10 minutes completes as duplicate.

use ilium_plugin_sdk::dedup;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::prelude::*;
use ilium_plugin_sdk::types::intents::SetDecorationSpec;

/// Sets the `hello` badge on one node. The key names the node and the change.
fn badge_submission(node: NodeId, change: &str) -> Submission {
    let node_text = format!("{node:?}");
    let intent = Intent::SetDecoration(SetDecorationSpec {
        node,
        slot: "hello".into(),
        content: vec![Span::plain("hi")],
        icon: None,
        sort_key: None,
        persist: false,
    });
    let key = dedup::key_for(&["badge", node_text.as_str(), change]);
    Submission::keyed(intent, key)
}

TypeScript: a client plugin that answers a command

This client-side plugin answers its own command with a desktop notice. The dedup key makes a second invocation within 10 minutes complete as duplicate.

import { definePlugin, type Event, type Submission } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk';
import { log } from '@ilium/plugin-sdk/host/log';

export const { lifecycle, handler } = definePlugin({
  side: 'client',
  activate(context) {
    log('info', `hello from ${context.plugin}`);
  },
  onEvents(batch: Event[]): Submission[] {
    const submissions: Submission[] = [];
    for (const event of batch) {
      if (event.tag !== 'command-invoked') continue;
      if (event.val.command !== 'com.example.hello/greet') continue;
      submissions.push({
        intent: {
          tag: 'notify',
          val: { title: 'Hello', body: 'from a plugin', urgency: 'normal', sound: undefined },
        },
        correlation: 1n,
        dedupKey: 'hello:greet',
      });
    }
    return submissions;
  },
});

Manifest: the grants for each side

Grants are listed per side. Each side has its own grant list, and the host checks each component against its own list.

"capabilities": {
  "server": ["agent.read", "tree.decorate", "fs.read:project"],
  "client": ["commands.invoke:com.example.hello/*"]
}

What the user sees

When a plugin's first activation needs high-risk grants, the host shows one prompt per plugin. The user can allow the selected grants or refuse for now. A refusal is asked again at the next server start, at most three times.

$ ilium plugin list
ok   example.demo 0.1.0  tier T2  sides server, client
err  example.hello-badge 0.1.1  stopped by the restart rule
     Stopped after 3 failures: handler.on-events trap.
     See notice N14 in Lifecycle.

Illustrative, not generated. A plugin list after the restart rule disabled one plugin.

Plugin example.hello-badge asks for:
  [x] agent.read
  [x] fs.read:project
  [ ] process.run:git        high risk

      [ Allow selected ]
      [ Not now ]

Illustrative, not generated. The grant prompt for a bundled plugin. fs.read:project is a normal-risk grant and starts checked. process.run:git is high risk and starts unchecked.

Edge cases

  • A refused submission does not reserve its dedup key, so a retry with the same key after fixing the cause is correct.
  • A submission that was accepted and then failed keeps its key. A retry of a failed action needs a new key.
  • A capability revoked during a call makes that call return revoked. The plugin is re-activated with the smaller grant set, and this is not a failure.
  • Three failures in 10 minutes disable a plugin on one side. The first failure restarts it after 1 s and the second after 5 s. The third disables it. Details: Lifecycle. A manual re-enable resets the count.

Component mode. A test mode in which the harness loads the built .wasm component in a WebAssembly runtime and enforces the limits. See Test harness reference.

Conformance case. One check of the conformance suite with a stable id such as CONF-LIFE-02. See Conformance suite.

Dev badge. The mark that Settings > Plugins and the plugin list show for a plugin installed by ilium plugin dev. See Debugging tools.

Expectation file. A JSON file next to a fixture that states the submissions, logs and outcomes the plugin must produce, with the match modes exact, ordered and subset. See Test harness reference.

FakeHost. The test double that stands in for the host for one plugin on one side. See Testing plugins.

FakeSession. The test double that runs several plugins, both sides and core extension point stubs in one fake session. See Test harness reference.

Fixture. A JSON file that sets the starting state of the fake host and lists events to deliver. See Test harness reference.

Golden file. A text file that holds the expected render of a view, compared by assert_golden. See Testing plugins.

Lint rule. A named, severity-ranked check of ilium plugin lint, such as lint.grant-unused. See Check and lint rules.

Native mode. A test mode in which the plugin runs as a plain library on the host machine, with no component and no enforced limits. See Test harness reference.

Replay file. A JSONL recording of the inputs of a session, written by trace --record and re-run by replay. See Test harness reference.

Snapshot. A stored value, pretty JSON with sorted keys, that a test compares with assert_snapshot. See Test harness reference.

Trace. The ring buffer of 1,024 records per plugin instance that shows events, submissions, host calls and outcomes. See Debugging tools.

Conventions

Correlation number. The u64 a plugin puts on a submission. Values below 2^63 belong to the plugin, values from 2^63 up to the SDK. See WIT reference conventions.

Dedup key. A string of 1 to 128 characters from [A-Za-z0-9._:/-] that makes a submission happen once within 10 minutes. See Intents.

epoch-ms. A u64 count of milliseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC. Durations are millisecond counts in fields that end in -ms.

Colour. A u32 written 0x00RRGGBB. The top byte is zero.

Id types. node-id, request-id, client-id, buffer-id and the other ids are unsigned integers that are opaque to the plugin.

Character limit. A limit in "characters" counts Unicode scalar values. A limit in "bytes" counts UTF-8 bytes.

Security

Audit log: security record of grants and policy events (Audit log). Admin policy: system TOML file that limits plugins (Admin policy). Project trust: user decision that a repository's .ilium/ values apply ([SEC-310]). Blocklist: signed list of banned packages ([SEC-146]). Safe mode: start with third-party code off ([SEC-328]). Data class: label for kind of data in a point field ([SEC-281]). Toxic combination: read grant plus egress grant ([SEC-004]). Key pinning: a package keeps its first signing key ([SEC-142]). Rotation statement: signed move to a new key ([SEC-143]).
